lessons.title: Close-up: the band and the carver

zoom.label: The foreground band: the player in white with his viol, left, beside the musicians' table

c1.text: Level one: a tradition says the band are painters. Zoom in on the player in white, at the front, with his viol.

zoom.label: The foreground band: the player in white with his viol, left, beside the musicians' table

c1q.text: Which painter does the old tradition see in him?

sources.title: Peter Bassano (Head of Brass, Royal College of Music), 'A Second Miracle at Cana: Recent Musical Discoveries in Veronese's Wedding Feast', Historic Brass Society Journal 6 (1994), pp. 11-18

Kate H. Hanson, 'The Language of the Banquet: Reconsidering Paolo Veronese's Wedding at Cana', InVisible Culture 14 (University of Rochester, 2010); cites D. Rosand, Painting in Cinquecento Venice (Cambridge UP, 1997), p. 122, and the contract as printed in J. Habert, Arte Veneta 44 (1993), pp. 89-90

Zygmunt Waźbiński, review of J. Habert and N. Volle, Les Noces de Cana de Véronèse. Une œuvre et sa restauration (Paris, RMN, 1992), Ochrona Zabytków 48/2 (1995), pp. 239-240 (Polish; our translations)

c1m.text: The man in white is Veronese by tradition: a lovely story, still argued over.

c1a.text: Yes. The 17th-century tradition makes him Veronese, painting himself into his own feast. Bassano backs it; the Louvre's 1992 study called the old names undocumented.

c1b.text: Titian is in the tradition's band, but not in white.

correction.tempting: Titian is the biggest name in the tradition's band, so he seems the obvious guess.
correction.truth: The tradition places Titian elsewhere in the band; the player in white is the one it calls Veronese.
correction.evidence: Bassano (1994), quoting the 1674 source: the one in white with the viola is Paolo himself. Hanson (2010): 'Veronese in white'.

c1c.text: Tintoretto is in the tradition too, just not in white.

correction.tempting: Tintoretto is one of the tradition's four names, so he's a fair guess.
correction.truth: The tradition calls the player in white Veronese; Tintoretto is said to be another player, and even that is doubted.
correction.evidence: Bassano (1994), citing Richard Cocke, doubts the Tintoretto name. Hanson (2010): 'Veronese in white'.

zoom.label: Behind the balustrade, directly above Christ's haloed head

c2.text: Level one: carver, Christ and hourglass share one line. Here's the top of it, just above Christ's head, behind the balustrade.

zoom.label: Behind the balustrade, directly above Christ's haloed head

c2q.text: What is the man up here doing?

sources.title: Kate H. Hanson, 'The Language of the Banquet: Reconsidering Paolo Veronese's Wedding at Cana', InVisible Culture 14 (University of Rochester, 2010); cites D. Rosand, Painting in Cinquecento Venice (Cambridge UP, 1997), p. 122, and the contract as printed in J. Habert, Arte Veneta 44 (1993), pp. 89-90
Mikeal C. Parsons and Heidi J. Hornik (Baylor University), 'Wedding at Cana, by Paolo Veronese', The Christian Century, 6 Jan 2016 issue ('On Art')
Peter Bassano (Head of Brass, Royal College of Music), 'A Second Miracle at Cana: Recent Musical Discoveries in Veronese's Wedding Feast', Historic Brass Society Journal 6 (1994), pp. 11-18

c2m.text: Carver above, Christ in the middle, hourglass below: one line, and one well-known reading.

c2a.text: The new wine is in the picture, but not up here.

correction.tempting: The new wine is the miracle, so a servant with a jug feels like the right guess.
correction.truth: Above Christ's head a servant chops meat; the new wine is tasted elsewhere, down in the crowd.
correction.evidence: Hanson (2010): a carver 'chops lamb' above Christ's head. Hornik and Parsons (2016): a servant 'slices meat' behind Christ.

c2b.text: Yes. A servant chops meat right above Christ's head. Rosand reads the carver-to-hourglass line as a hint of sacrifice; Hornik and Parsons ask, 'Lamb of God?'

c2c.text: The music is lower down, in the foreground.

correction.tempting: The band sits on the same central line, so music up here would fit the pattern.
correction.truth: The band plays in the foreground below Christ; up here, behind the balustrade, a servant carves meat.
correction.evidence: Bassano (1994): the musicians in the foreground, below Christ. Hanson, and Hornik and Parsons: meat carved above and behind Christ.

extends.concept: The band and the 17th-century tradition that names them as painters

c1q.what_you_learn: The player in white is the one the 17th-century tradition calls Veronese; Titian and Tintoretto are other players in that tradition, and the identifications are debated.
